Cc: Anand Patel <anand.patel@adops.io>
Date: Mon, 03 May 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Questions on SDK pixel, consent flags, and data residency

Hi Sergio,

Thanks for the demo last week — BrightAd's web team is ready to start a small pilot with Redwood's client-side SDK for pageview telemetry and conversion pixel firing. Before we move ahead our privacy and legal teams asked for quick clarification on implementation details so we can map the consent flow to our CMP. A few concrete items: 

- Does the Redwood SDK read or write first-party cookies by default, or can it be configured to be cookie-less?
- If we use the SDK with default settings, what precise categories of personal data are sent to Redwood (e.g., IP, user agent, device identifiers, hashed email)?
- Can we toggle telemetry collection server-side vs client-side so consent is enforced before any outbound call?
- For EU users, is telemetry routed to EU-only endpoints to avoid cross-border transfers, or does your hosted offering require transfers to US data centers?

We also need to know whether enabling "anonymous mode" (as described briefly during the demo) strips IP addresses before they leave the browser or whether that happens in your backend.

Appreciate a short note we can pass to our privacy lead — we want to keep the pilot moving this month.

Best,
Kate

Subject: Re: Questions on SDK pixel, consent flags, and data residency

Hi Kate — great to hear the pilot is kicking off. Quick replies below; looping in Laura (Legal) and Marissa (Product) for anything I miss.

- Cookie use: Redwood's browser SDK can operate in two modes. Default mode sets a first-party session cookie to help de-dupe events across tabs; however you can disable cookies entirely and rely on randomized client IDs.

- Data sent: by default the SDK sends timestamp, event name, page URL, user agent string, and IP address. We do not collect clear-text emails from the browser unless you explicitly pass them as event properties; hashing on the client is supported.

- Consent enforcement: you can (A) gate network calls in the SDK so it doesn't emit until your CMP grants marketing consent, or (B) send to your backend and let Redwood accept only server-side-sent events. Option A is recommended for lower latency but requires CMP integration client-side.

- EU routing: our hosted control plane supports regional endpoints; for the pilot we can configure the SDK to send telemetry to eu.api.redwood.inference which keeps EU events within EU regions. Note: some background processing (indexing/analytics) may touch other regions unless you sign the Dedicated/Private contract.

- Anonymous mode: if you enable 'client-anonymize' the SDK strips/obfuscates IP on the client prior to dispatch. If left off, IP is sent and redacted in our backend according to retention settings. 

I'll attach the public DPA and the current subprocessors inventory for your privacy team. Laura — can you confirm the above wording and add any legal caveats on our side?

Next step: Kate, would you prefer a 20-minute call with your privacy lead or shall we provide a short one-page technical memo?

Thanks,
Sergio Alvarez

Subject: Re: Questions on SDK pixel, consent flags, and data residency

Hi Kate — quick legal clarifications below, short and focused so you can share with your privacy lead: 

1) Data categories: for standard telemetry we process pseudonymous identifiers, device and request metadata, and event content you choose to include. We expressly do not ingest customer PII from our SDK unless you pass it. If you need Redwood to process hashed identifiers as "personal data" under your legal model, note that will be treated accordingly in the DPA.

2) Subprocessors & transfers: the subprocessors list we attached shows storage and observability providers. For BrightAd's EU users, routing to eu.api.redwood.inference avoids transfer of the raw event stream to the US. However, certain admin and analytics jobs may replicate telemetry metadata to our centralized services; if you require full EU residency we should evaluate Redwood Private or a Dedicated contract and add a contract clause for restricted processing.

3) Technical controls: suggest two mitigation options for the pilot — (i) enable client-side anonymization (SDK option) so IPs are truncated before leaving the browser, and (ii) configure the SDK to send minimal payloads (no user_id/email). Both are supported immediately.

4) Documentation & evidence: we've attached the DPA and the current subprocessors inventory. If required for procurement we can also provide SOC 2 Type II summary and a scoped transfer impact assessment.

If helpful I can join a 20-minute call with your privacy lead tomorrow afternoon.

Regards,
Laura Bennett
Senior Counsel, Privacy & Compliance
